Eggsploitation - International Egg Donation

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
promises free overseas holidays lure young women to donate their eggs... the exploitation and life threatening risks often omitted.

Summary:
One in four couples in developing countries had been found to be affected by infertility. This translates to millions of couples requiring some kind of assisted reproduction treatment.

Globally, fertility treatment has become increasingly popular solution for couples battling to conceive a child of their own with egg donation agencies popping up all over the world. Offering young women an opportunity to sell their eggs in lieu of an exciting overseas trip.

But reality is far from a dream holiday. We bring you the story of a young woman that donated her eggs and almost became infertile herself.

Further information:
THE BIG SELL

A Free trip to India or Nepal, sightseeing, hotel accommodation, meals and flights included PLUS spending money and the opportunity to help a couple start a family.

Online ads targeting young women between the ages of 18-26 to donate their eggs abroad, specifically India, Nepal and Thailand are becoming more and more common on the internet – and South AFrican women are responding.

“I went to India to do something good, and came back the victim of a system” – Annika Malan, 20.

EGG DONATION

These fertility egg donation programmes raise a host of uncomfortable questions that touch on morals and modern science, exploitation and globalization, and that most natural of desires: to have a family.

According to Lizanne van Waart – a specialised infertility psychologist – egg donation is a wonderful things when it’s doen for the right reasons and in the right way, with experienced professionals who respect egg donations laws and guidelines. Lizanne has worked in India herself and has seen the conditions first hand. She says, in the wrong hands it can leave women both physically and psychologically damaged. A number of the women have returned from their promised holiday with serious complications which are mostly the result of over-stimulation caused by incorrect administration of hormone medicines.

ANNIKA’s STORY
Annika Malan, 20, a second year BCOm student at Stellenbosch University was approached on Facebook by a “friendly young woman who got chatting” then sent her an egg donor agency ad. Annika thought it sounded fantastic. But what was not speeld out was exactly what she needed to do – and the dangers!

Annika flew to India on her complimentary return ticket in August 2015. Initially impressed with the attention and support she received, she was excited to be traveling internationally. The hotel met her expectations and the clinic looked fine. She was told about the kind of couple she’d be helping to conceive – so she was happy to do it.

The donation procedure was more daunting than she had expected. Over two weeks she was dosed with meds to help produce the additonal eggs for harvesting. She was then flown from Hyderabad in India to Katmandu for the “second part of the holiday” and the aspiration of the eggs. After the procedure she came to about an hour later and was dropped off at the hotel – it was over she was told. But two days later, her abdomen hurt and she felt bloated – unable to eat, urinate or breathe – she contacted the clinic doctor but was told he couldn’t help. She contacted the agent that arranged the trip and got the same response. Shocked and disappointed that the same people that were so helpful cut all contact when she fell ill. Terrified and in agony she took a taxi to the airport and flew home. She was rushed to hospital on arrival and hospitalised with severe ovarian hyper stimulation syndrome (OHSS) – a life-threatening condition.

After several days in ICU she responded to medical treatment and the removal of fluid from her abdomen and chest – she recovered soon afterwards. She was fortunate – some women have lost their ovaries leaving them infertile.

But Annika’s psychological hurt persisted and she is still in therapy. Infertility Psychologist, Lizanne, says this is common amongst young donors. They worry about whether they will be able to conceive themselves and have their own children one day. Fears arise about where their eggs will end up. Deep regret emerges, and sometimes the symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder present themselves, as in Annika’s case.

LAURA's STORY
Laura Skye went to India with the same altruistic intentions as Annika a few years ago. She wanted to help couples conceive their own families. After the procedure she was in immense pain, but was discharged and taken back to the hotel. Hours later Laura was flown back to South Africa. She was rushed straight to hospital and underwent a series of surgeries - her ovaries had ruptured as a result of over-stimulation - she was bleeding internally. She was at death's door, the irony that in her effort to help give life she was at risk of losing hers. Today, her chances of being able to conceive a child herself are slim to none. Laura has agreed to share her story and will show her face.

INTERNATIONAL DEMAND & LEGALITY
In many first world countries where the availability of of contraception and access to safe abortions have greatly lowered the number of babies available for adoption, the demand for egg donation is growing.

Donation is illegal in a number of countries including Italy and Germany, while there are waiting lists of women wanting eggs in the Uk and South Africa. Lizanne says, this demand has fostered an illegal international market in which desperate couples are prepared to pay for eggs.

International law prohibits payment for any live human matter, including eggs and sperm. But because the procedure for harvestign eggs is time-consuming and causes discomfort, donors can be reimbursed for their time and medical bills – creating a loop hole. With the advent of egg-freezing technology, Lizanne says there’s a growin risk of donated eggs not going to recipients based on proper scientific matching but rahter that the eggs are being sold to centain egg banks to be used as they choose, despite it being against the law.

In countries such as India, where the IVF industry is largely unregulated and has become commercialised and some unscrupulous doctors and clinic attempt to improve their proficts by overdosing donors with hormones to icnrease their harvest of eggs. They use agents to lure donors with the promsie of exotic holidays and sometimes straight up cash.

They appear to be targeting the UK, SA and Ukraine for donors.

INDUSTRY INSIDER - HIDDEN IDENTITY
We have a leading international fertility expert that globally inspects and accredits fertility clinics who is willing to give us an interview provided we hide her identity - as she is very well known in the industry and she fears that her speaking out about what she has seen in India will jeopardise her employment. She is currently based in Australia and will do a telephonic interview with me. I will film an actor for the on-screen representation. Below is an extract from her email:
"I was in India doing the same as I do I South Africa and many other places. I have long refused to go to India due to ethical concerns but was convinced and promised that they would choose only ethically sound centres for me. This was not true and what I got to see and experience is horrific beyond words and scarred me for life. I had nightmares and had to have counselling afterwards.
I guess part of my therapy has been to share what I experienced with many others…..

Three Ukrainian girls at one of the centres who had a very high number of eggs picked up on the day of my visit all showing clear signs of OHSS and all booked to fly back to Ukraine the very same day. I was pleading with the doctor in charge saying these girls (especially one) could die during a flight and she should not fly – but I was met with the attitude of not my problem…."

MEDICAL RISKS
The procedure: An oral contraceptive pill is given, followed by two weeks of twice-daily hormone injections to stimulate the folliciles to produce considerably more than the one ripevovum they usually produce each month. This can result in bloating and mood swings. The harvesting involves beign injected with a triggering agent and anesthetic. Once the donor is sedated, a needle is inserted through the abdomen into the ovaries to suck up the ripe eggs.

The biggest medical problem is ovarian hyper stimulation syndrome (OHSS), a condition that affects only two percent of donors at accredited facilities, but it is a far greater risk when hormone doses are hiked up to produce more eggs for harvest – in some cases as many as 30, instead of the usual eight to 12 in accredited South African clinics.

With OHSS, excess fluid moves from blood vessels to the tissue and spaces between the lungs and in the abdomen, causing difficulty breathing and extreme discomfort. The risk is real. Ovaries can swell to 12 times their normal size at the risk of twisting on their stalks and losing their blood supply – a condition that requires urgent surgery and may result in the loss of the organ. In the worst cases, OHSS can result in renal failure, respiratory and general systematic organ failure and death.

Another feared complication is infection with sepsis and the formation of abscesses in the ovarian tubes that requires surgical removal of the ovaries as a result of poor technique and non-sterile clinics where the harvesting is preformed.

Psychologist Lizanne says the bottom line is young women should avoid traveling overseas to donate their eggs - the risk outweighs the reward.

Press Release:


Eggsploitation
Unsuspecting young South African women are heading overseas to donate their eggs to infertile couples and earn a free international holiday in the process. But, at what cost? Carte Blanche exposes the ugly truth behind global egg donation agencies robbing women of their chances of ever having their own babies.


Script:


CROSS BORDER EGG DONATION STRUCTURE

VO: Infertility affects one in six couples. With Millions of people needing assisted reproductive treatment - it has given rise to a fertility industry worth billions of rands globally.

DALMEYER: Our genetic pool is a very strong genetic pool and South African eggs are very in demand in the first world.

VO: This demand, fosters an illegal international network where human tissue is traded for cold hard cash on the black market.

ANIEKA: I walked in as a hero and I left as victim. They literally harvested me, they took me for everything that I was there for, that hurt me, I was angry.

LINK: Dodgy agencies sell young women an idealistic dream, a chance to change lives by giving life and in return they are rewarded with an exciting overseas trip, and money.

VO: It’s a big sell. Online ads target young women between the ages of 18 and 26 to donate their eggs abroad, in countries like India, Nepal and Thailand. South African women are signing up.

Twenty-one year, Economics student Anieka Malan, always wanted to donate her egg to help an infertile couple start a family.

She thought it was a sign when she was contacted on Facebook last year.

ANIEKA: I was like Joh! I really want to see India and it’s something I really wanted to do. I immediately responded. It looked really legit.
CLAIRE: What was the deal?
ANIEKA: You get to go to India, // you get you stay in a very, very fancy 5 star hotel, you get travelled around, you don’t pay for anything, you get pocket money.

VO: But the reality would be far from the dream that was sold to Anieka.

Specialised infertility psychologist, Lizanne van Waart say she has seen an increase in cross border horror cases.

LIZANNE: This is not a game, this is not a money game, it’s not about a holiday - it’s not about eggs we’re donating, it’s something we must take seriously.

VO: International law prohibits payment for any live human matter, which includes eggs and sperm for reproductive treatment. But unscrupulous agencies have found loopholes.

The procedure for harvesting eggs is time-consuming and causes discomfort. Donors are “reimbursed” for their time and medical bills to the tune of between 7 and 10000 rand. Throw in an exotic holiday and young women are lining up – often unaware of the real risks of cross border egg donation.



LIZANNE: They have no idea they clinics are looking like on the other side. Your eggs are going to be commercialised you don’t know where your eggs are going at all.

VO: Laura Skye signed up for egg donation in 2011, at 21, it was a decision motivated by a family member’s struggle to fall pregnant. Despite doing research she says she was not prepared for how her life would be changed.

LAURA: I tried to help people give life and in the process I nearly lost mine, and now I might never be able to produce my own life – is that worth it? Have I destroyed any hope of ever being called a mom? I don’t know

VO: Initially Laura thought she’d be donating in South Africa.

LAURA: I always thought it would be here. It was only when I told that there was a couple that really wanted a baby and they only way they could do was through a surrogate in India, that is the only way I was ok with it, when I heard their story

VO: Egg donation is a wonderful gift, and is a safe medical procedure provided it is done in a regulated environment, says Dr. Paul Dalmeyer from the Southern African Society of Reproductive Medicine and Gynaecological Endoscopy.

CLAIRE: What physically happens to a woman’s body during egg donation?
DALMEYER: They are hormonally manipulated to over-stimulate the ovaries so that these ovaries can produce more eggs than normal.

LINK: In South Africa, to be safe, the number of eggs harvested is limited to around 15, but in some developing countries harvests go up to 30 or even 60 eggs per donor – pushing the limits and the profits.

DALMEYER: If there is financial gain, ethics and morals go out the back door . They are very poorly regulated. In good hands the risks are low, in bad hands the risks are there.

VO: One of the medical complications young women are open to, is Ovarian Hyper Stimulation Syndrome - egg production goes into overdrive mode – although these cases are rare, it can be fatal.

DALMEYER: They run into respiratory problems, where they have sepsis, we have thrombo embolic events, you have renal complications, you torsions of the ovaries, the complications are serious.

VO: Lizanne points out that with different fertility legislation around the world, donor’s rights also differ from one country to the next.

LIZANNE: They never been informed what will happen to them. Nothing about the regulations, nothing about the consent forms, what law apply - nothing about what will happen to you.

VO: Laura says her heart hit the floor when she walked into the theatre in India. There was a bucket of bloody gauze by the bed.

LAURA: at that point I felt like cattle, I felt like I was being herded through a cattle prod and they were just tagging, tagging, taking eggs, next, taking eggs, next. I was scared, I was white, I was shaking.

VO: For Anieka, the fear struck only after her procedure. She was treated to a fantastic holiday in India, and then sent to Nepal for her egg donation. She says the clinic looked fine, but when she woke up, she realised everything was far from fine.

ANIEKA: I was in such pain, and my lung, actually, screaming because I was in such pain

VO: Laure woke up in a similar situation in India.

LAURA: It was just flashes of pain, I’m going back under and then I’m coming to. Everyone is telling me I’m fine, and I’m telling them my body is telling me I am not fine. I was terrified, my abdomen started swelling, I was sick, I was throwing up.

VO: Both young women were experiencing severe ovarian hyper stimulation syndrome - this should have raised concern for the doctors, but in both cases, they were given basic pain medication and discharged.

ANIEKA: That night, I was lying in a foreign country, in a foreign hotel room, by myself alone, I had no one there, and I was just lying there in pain.

VO: Unable to reach the doctors, Anieka felt abandoned. Eventually one of the surgeons responded and gave her more pain medication. She was put on a plane back to South Africa the next day.

ANIEKA: My belly was swollen, I had blue marks over my entire body, my one lung had collapsed and it was really excruciating. INT 2 M5

DALMEYER: It’s a medical principle that if you have a potential complication, that the patient has got to managed straight away. If you don’t pick up those cases very quickly they land up with all sorts of surgical complication, and probably infertility as well.

VO: A reality, cross border donors often only face when they get emergency treatment back in South Africa.

Laura’s ovaries had ruptured – she had been bleeding internally for three days since the procedure in India – she was rushed to surgery.

LAURA: I was thinking, what was going to happen, I was bleeding on the inside, are they going to take everything out, are they? What’s … I was terrified.

VO: Laura would come out of the surgery with a permanent reminder of her egg donation.

LAURA: they had to take two litres of infected blood out of abdomen and deflate my ovaries. I have a scar about that long going down from my belly button to my pubic bone.

VO: With the trauma of the surgery and subsequent scar tissue that developed, Laura’s chances of falling pregnant one day, are limited.

LAURA: The most ironic thing had happened, I was in so much pain, I actually said to myself, if this is the kind of pain women talk about giving birth, I never want to give birth. I hate myself for thinking that.

VO: A deep sense of regret and Post Traumatic Stress disorder is not uncommon for young cross border donors. Lizanne has treated at least 15 South African women in the last year.

LIZANNE: the psychological and emotional burden is quite high and they really struggle to cope with that afterwards.

VO: But Laura blames the process, not the cause.

LAURA: It’s a good cause, and it still it is, I would never tell someone not to do it, I would say please do your research, please make sure you’re doing it the right way, for the right reasons, because there are consequences. And I live with those consequences every single day.

VO: Anieka’s recovery took two months, she will be able to have children one day. Emotionally, she believes she has grown through the experience.

ANIEKA: everything feels right and in place and I know that this happen to me for a reason
CLAIRE: Do you know if there were pregnancies from your donation?
ANIEKA: I know nothing, I have no control over it, and that doesn’t bother me at all, I’ve made peace with that.

VO: Currently there is no legislation guiding cross border egg donation. Agencies are unregulated and often make a run for it for when things go wrong. Dr. Dalmeyer tried to contact the agent Anieka dealt with.

DALMEYER: I could not raise that individual, I phoned the clinic in India, disappeared, the clinician wouldn’t speak to me – from a medical man to a medical man.

VO: Laura’s agency has closed. She was told that her donation resulted in pregnancies and healthy babies were born. Something she holds on to, now that her own chances conceiving are uncertain…

LAURA: That makes me feel a bit better about my situation, that somewhere in the world, I helped and it was worth it and if it wasn’t and all of that happened for nothing, for absolutely nothing, it would destroy me.



PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: Overseas holidays in exchange for egg donation to help infertile couples – pushing medical limits and profits.

LAURA: I felt like I was being herded through a cattle prod and they were just tagging, tagging, taking eggs, next, taking eggs, next….

PROMO 2
VO: Cross border egg donation agencies target South African women, luring them with exotic holidays, and cash.

ANIEKA: They literally harvested me, they took me for everything that I was there for, that hurt me, I was angry.

VO: Does risk outweighs the reward?

PROMO 3 – 10 seconds
VO: A chance to give life through cross border egg donation – but at what cost?

LAURA: Have I destroyed any hope of ever being called a mom? I don’t know

WARR/NICK BARDONI KPM 0192 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 10 April 2016 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 21 April 2016 Press Release: Eggsploitation Unsuspecting young South African women are heading overseas to donate their eggs to infertile couples and earn a free international holiday in the process. But, at what cost? Carte Blanche exposes the ugly truth behind global egg donation agencies robbing women of their chances of ever having their own babies. Script: CROSS BORDER EGG DONATION STRUCTURE VO: Infertility affects one in six couples. With Millions of people needing assisted reproductive treatment - it has given rise to a fertility industry worth billions of rands globally. DALMEYER: Our genetic pool is a very strong genetic pool and South African eggs are very in demand in the first world. VO: This demand, fosters an illegal international network where human tissue is traded for cold hard cash on the black market. ANIEKA: I walked in as a hero and I left as victim. They literally harvested me, they took me for everything that I was there for, that hurt me, I was angry. LINK: Dodgy agencies sell young women an idealistic dream, a chance to change lives by giving life and in return they are rewarded with an exciting overseas trip, and money. VO: It’s a big sell. Online ads target young women between the ages of 18 and 26 to donate their eggs abroad, in countries like India, Nepal and Thailand. South African women are signing up. Twenty-one year, Economics student Anieka Malan, always wanted to donate her egg to help an infertile couple start a family. She thought it was a sign when she was contacted on Facebook last year. ANIEKA: I was like Joh! I really want to see India and it’s something I really wanted to do. I immediately responded. It looked really legit. CLAIRE: What was the deal? ANIEKA: You get to go to India, // you get you stay in a very, very fancy 5 star hotel, you get travelled around, you don’t pay for anything, you get pocket money. VO: But the reality would be far from the dream that was sold to Anieka. Specialised infertility psychologist, Lizanne van Waart say she has seen an increase in cross border horror cases. LIZANNE: This is not a game, this is not a money game, it’s not about a holiday - it’s not about eggs we’re donating, it’s something we must take seriously. VO: International law prohibits payment for any live human matter, which includes eggs and sperm for reproductive treatment. But unscrupulous agencies have found loopholes. The procedure for harvesting eggs is time-consuming and causes discomfort. Donors are “reimbursed” for their time and medical bills to the tune of between 7 and 10000 rand. Throw in an exotic holiday and young women are lining up – often unaware of the real risks of cross border egg donation. LIZANNE: They have no idea they clinics are looking like on the other side. Your eggs are going to be commercialised you don’t know where your eggs are going at all. VO: Laura Skye signed up for egg donation in 2011, at 21, it was a decision motivated by a family member’s struggle to fall pregnant. Despite doing research she says she was not prepared for how her life would be changed. LAURA: I tried to help people give life and in the process I nearly lost mine, and now I might never be able to produce my own life – is that worth it? Have I destroyed any hope of ever being called a mom? I don’t know VO: Initially Laura thought she’d be donating in South Africa. LAURA: I always thought it would be here. It was only when I told that there was a couple that really wanted a baby and they only way they could do was through a surrogate in India, that is the only way I was ok with it, when I heard their story VO: Egg donation is a wonderful gift, and is a safe medical procedure provided it is done in a regulated environment, says Dr. Paul Dalmeyer from the Southern African Society of Reproductive Medicine and Gynaecological Endoscopy. CLAIRE: What physically happens to a woman’s body during egg donation? DALMEYER: They are hormonally manipulated to over-stimulate the ovaries so that these ovaries can produce more eggs than normal. LINK: In South Africa, to be safe, the number of eggs harvested is limited to around 15, but in some developing countries harvests go up to 30 or even 60 eggs per donor – pushing the limits and the profits. DALMEYER: If there is financial gain, ethics and morals go out the back door . They are very poorly regulated. In good hands the risks are low, in bad hands the risks are there. VO: One of the medical complications young women are open to, is Ovarian Hyper Stimulation Syndrome - egg production goes into overdrive mode – although these cases are rare, it can be fatal. DALMEYER: They run into respiratory problems, where they have sepsis, we have thrombo embolic events, you have renal complications, you torsions of the ovaries, the complications are serious. VO: Lizanne points out that with different fertility legislation around the world, donor’s rights also differ from one country to the next. LIZANNE: They never been informed what will happen to them. Nothing about the regulations, nothing about the consent forms, what law apply - nothing about what will happen to you. VO: Laura says her heart hit the floor when she walked into the theatre in India. There was a bucket of bloody gauze by the bed. LAURA: at that point I felt like cattle, I felt like I was being herded through a cattle prod and they were just tagging, tagging, taking eggs, next, taking eggs, next. I was scared, I was white, I was shaking. VO: For Anieka, the fear struck only after her procedure. She was treated to a fantastic holiday in India, and then sent to Nepal for her egg donation. She says the clinic looked fine, but when she woke up, she realised everything was far from fine. ANIEKA: I was in such pain, and my lung, actually, screaming because I was in such pain VO: Laure woke up in a similar situation in India. LAURA: It was just flashes of pain, I’m going back under and then I’m coming to. Everyone is telling me I’m fine, and I’m telling them my body is telling me I am not fine. I was terrified, my abdomen started swelling, I was sick, I was throwing up. VO: Both young women were experiencing severe ovarian hyper stimulation syndrome - this should have raised concern for the doctors, but in both cases, they were given basic pain medication and discharged. ANIEKA: That night, I was lying in a foreign country, in a foreign hotel room, by myself alone, I had no one there, and I was just lying there in pain. VO: Unable to reach the doctors, Anieka felt abandoned. Eventually one of the surgeons responded and gave her more pain medication. She was put on a plane back to South Africa the next day. ANIEKA: My belly was swollen, I had blue marks over my entire body, my one lung had collapsed and it was really excruciating. INT 2 M5 DALMEYER: It’s a medical principle that if you have a potential complication, that the patient has got to managed straight away. If you don’t pick up those cases very quickly they land up with all sorts of surgical complication, and probably infertility as well. VO: A reality, cross border donors often only face when they get emergency treatment back in South Africa. Laura’s ovaries had ruptured – she had been bleeding internally for three days since the procedure in India – she was rushed to surgery. LAURA: I was thinking, what was going to happen, I was bleeding on the inside, are they going to take everything out, are they? What’s … I was terrified. VO: Laura would come out of the surgery with a permanent reminder of her egg donation. LAURA: they had to take two litres of infected blood out of abdomen and deflate my ovaries. I have a scar about that long going down from my belly button to my pubic bone. VO: With the trauma of the surgery and subsequent scar tissue that developed, Laura’s chances of falling pregnant one day, are limited. LAURA: The most ironic thing had happened, I was in so much pain, I actually said to myself, if this is the kind of pain women talk about giving birth, I never want to give birth. I hate myself for thinking that. VO: A deep sense of regret and Post Traumatic Stress disorder is not uncommon for young cross border donors. Lizanne has treated at least 15 South African women in the last year. LIZANNE: the psychological and emotional burden is quite high and they really struggle to cope with that afterwards. VO: But Laura blames the process, not the cause. LAURA: It’s a good cause, and it still it is, I would never tell someone not to do it, I would say please do your research, please make sure you’re doing it the right way, for the right reasons, because there are consequences. And I live with those consequences every single day. VO: Anieka’s recovery took two months, she will be able to have children one day. Emotionally, she believes she has grown through the experience. ANIEKA: everything feels right and in place and I know that this happen to me for a reason CLAIRE: Do you know if there were pregnancies from your donation? ANIEKA: I know nothing, I have no control over it, and that doesn’t bother me at all, I’ve made peace with that. VO: Currently there is no legislation guiding cross border egg donation. Agencies are unregulated and often make a run for it for when things go wrong. Dr. Dalmeyer tried to contact the agent Anieka dealt with. DALMEYER: I could not raise that individual, I phoned the clinic in India, disappeared, the clinician wouldn’t speak to me – from a medical man to a medical man. VO: Laura’s agency has closed. She was told that her donation resulted in pregnancies and healthy babies were born. Something she holds on to, now that her own chances conceiving are uncertain… LAURA: That makes me feel a bit better about my situation, that somewhere in the world, I helped and it was worth it and if it wasn’t and all of that happened for nothing, for absolutely nothing, it would destroy me. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: Overseas holidays in exchange for egg donation to help infertile couples – pushing medical limits and profits. LAURA: I felt like I was being herded through a cattle prod and they were just tagging, tagging, taking eggs, next, taking eggs, next…. PROMO 2 VO: Cross border egg donation agencies target South African women, luring them with exotic holidays, and cash. ANIEKA: They literally harvested me, they took me for everything that I was there for, that hurt me, I was angry. VO: Does risk outweighs the reward? PROMO 3 – 10 seconds VO: A chance to give life through cross border egg donation – but at what cost? LAURA: Have I destroyed any hope of ever being called a mom? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): promises free overseas holidays lure young women to donate their eggs... the exploitation and life threatening risks often omitted.
metadata.Summary: One in four couples in developing countries had been found to be affected by infertility. This translates to millions of couples requiring some kind of assisted reproduction treatment. Globally, fertility treatment has become increasingly popular solution for couples battling to conceive a child of their own with egg donation agencies popping up all over the world. Offering young women an opportunity to sell their eggs in lieu of an exciting overseas trip. But reality is far from a dream holiday. We bring you the story of a young woman that donated her eggs and almost became infertile herself.
metadata.Further information: THE BIG SELL A Free trip to India or Nepal, sightseeing, hotel accommodation, meals and flights included PLUS spending money and the opportunity to help a couple start a family. Online ads targeting young women between the ages of 18-26 to donate their eggs abroad, specifically India, Nepal and Thailand are becoming more and more common on the internet – and South AFrican women are responding. “I went to India to do something good, and came back the victim of a system” – Annika Malan, 20. EGG DONATION These fertility egg donation programmes raise a host of uncomfortable questions that touch on morals and modern science, exploitation and globalization, and that most natural of desires: to have a family. According to Lizanne van Waart – a specialised infertility psychologist – egg donation is a wonderful things when it’s doen for the right reasons and in the right way, with experienced professionals who respect egg donations laws and guidelines. Lizanne has worked in India herself and has seen the conditions first hand. She says, in the wrong hands it can leave women both physically and psychologically damaged. A number of the women have returned from their promised holiday with serious complications which are mostly the result of over-stimulation caused by incorrect administration of hormone medicines. ANNIKA’s STORY Annika Malan, 20, a second year BCOm student at Stellenbosch University was approached on Facebook by a “friendly young woman who got chatting” then sent her an egg donor agency ad. Annika thought it sounded fantastic. But what was not speeld out was exactly what she needed to do – and the dangers! Annika flew to India on her complimentary return ticket in August 2015. Initially impressed with the attention and support she received, she was excited to be traveling internationally. The hotel met her expectations and the clinic looked fine. She was told about the kind of couple she’d be helping to conceive – so she was happy to do it. The donation procedure was more daunting than she had expected. Over two weeks she was dosed with meds to help produce the additonal eggs for harvesting. She was then flown from Hyderabad in India to Katmandu for the “second part of the holiday” and the aspiration of the eggs. After the procedure she came to about an hour later and was dropped off at the hotel – it was over she was told. But two days later, her abdomen hurt and she felt bloated – unable to eat, urinate or breathe – she contacted the clinic doctor but was told he couldn’t help. She contacted the agent that arranged the trip and got the same response. Shocked and disappointed that the same people that were so helpful cut all contact when she fell ill. Terrified and in agony she took a taxi to the airport and flew home. She was rushed to hospital on arrival and hospitalised with severe ovarian hyper stimulation syndrome (OHSS) – a life-threatening condition. After several days in ICU she responded to medical treatment and the removal of fluid from her abdomen and chest – she recovered soon afterwards. She was fortunate – some women have lost their ovaries leaving them infertile. But Annika’s psychological hurt persisted and she is still in therapy. Infertility Psychologist, Lizanne, says this is common amongst young donors. They worry about whether they will be able to conceive themselves and have their own children one day. Fears arise about where their eggs will end up. Deep regret emerges, and sometimes the symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder present themselves, as in Annika’s case. LAURA's STORY Laura Skye went to India with the same altruistic intentions as Annika a few years ago. She wanted to help couples conceive their own families. After the procedure she was in immense pain, but was discharged and taken back to the hotel. Hours later Laura was flown back to South Africa. She was rushed straight to hospital and underwent a series of surgeries - her ovaries had ruptured as a result of over-stimulation - she was bleeding internally. She was at death's door, the irony that in her effort to help give life she was at risk of losing hers. Today, her chances of being able to conceive a child herself are slim to none. Laura has agreed to share her story and will show her face. INTERNATIONAL DEMAND & LEGALITY In many first world countries where the availability of of contraception and access to safe abortions have greatly lowered the number of babies available for adoption, the demand for egg donation is growing. Donation is illegal in a number of countries including Italy and Germany, while there are waiting lists of women wanting eggs in the Uk and South Africa. Lizanne says, this demand has fostered an illegal international market in which desperate couples are prepared to pay for eggs. International law prohibits payment for any live human matter, including eggs and sperm. But because the procedure for harvestign eggs is time-consuming and causes discomfort, donors can be reimbursed for their time and medical bills – creating a loop hole. With the advent of egg-freezing technology, Lizanne says there’s a growin risk of donated eggs not going to recipients based on proper scientific matching but rahter that the eggs are being sold to centain egg banks to be used as they choose, despite it being against the law. In countries such as India, where the IVF industry is largely unregulated and has become commercialised and some unscrupulous doctors and clinic attempt to improve their proficts by overdosing donors with hormones to icnrease their harvest of eggs. They use agents to lure donors with the promsie of exotic holidays and sometimes straight up cash. They appear to be targeting the UK, SA and Ukraine for donors. INDUSTRY INSIDER - HIDDEN IDENTITY We have a leading international fertility expert that globally inspects and accredits fertility clinics who is willing to give us an interview provided we hide her identity - as she is very well known in the industry and she fears that her speaking out about what she has seen in India will jeopardise her employment. She is currently based in Australia and will do a telephonic interview with me. I will film an actor for the on-screen representation. Below is an extract from her email: "I was in India doing the same as I do I South Africa and many other places. I have long refused to go to India due to ethical concerns but was convinced and promised that they would choose only ethically sound centres for me. This was not true and what I got to see and experience is horrific beyond words and scarred me for life. I had nightmares and had to have counselling afterwards. I guess part of my therapy has been to share what I experienced with many others….. Three Ukrainian girls at one of the centres who had a very high number of eggs picked up on the day of my visit all showing clear signs of OHSS and all booked to fly back to Ukraine the very same day. I was pleading with the doctor in charge saying these girls (especially one) could die during a flight and she should not fly – but I was met with the attitude of not my problem…." MEDICAL RISKS The procedure: An oral contraceptive pill is given, followed by two weeks of twice-daily hormone injections to stimulate the folliciles to produce considerably more than the one ripevovum they usually produce each month. This can result in bloating and mood swings. The harvesting involves beign injected with a triggering agent and anesthetic. Once the donor is sedated, a needle is inserted through the abdomen into the ovaries to suck up the ripe eggs. The biggest medical problem is ovarian hyper stimulation syndrome (OHSS), a condition that affects only two percent of donors at accredited facilities, but it is a far greater risk when hormone doses are hiked up to produce more eggs for harvest – in some cases as many as 30, instead of the usual eight to 12 in accredited South African clinics. With OHSS, excess fluid moves from blood vessels to the tissue and spaces between the lungs and in the abdomen, causing difficulty breathing and extreme discomfort. The risk is real. Ovaries can swell to 12 times their normal size at the risk of twisting on their stalks and losing their blood supply – a condition that requires urgent surgery and may result in the loss of the organ. In the worst cases, OHSS can result in renal failure, respiratory and general systematic organ failure and death. Another feared complication is infection with sepsis and the formation of abscesses in the ovarian tubes that requires surgical removal of the ovaries as a result of poor technique and non-sterile clinics where the harvesting is preformed. Psychologist Lizanne says the bottom line is young women should avoid traveling overseas to donate their eggs - the risk outweighs the reward.
